title: Kushari
subtitle: Egyptian street food with rice, lentils, pasta, and spiced tomato sauce
excerpt: Kushari is Egypt's national street food: a heaped plate of rice, brown lentils, pasta, and chickpeas topped with a sharp, spiced tomato sauce and finished with a pour of crisp fried onion in vinegar. It sounds improbable and tastes extraordinary. The competing textures and the hot-sour combination make it completely addictive.
sourceNotes: Kushari (also koshary or koshari) is considered the national dish of Egypt. It is sold at specialist kushari shops across Cairo and Alexandria, where each component is cooked separately and assembled to order. The dish dates to the nineteenth century and shows Indian, Italian, and Middle Eastern influences.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Each component keeps well. Store separately and assemble fresh when serving.

content.text: Kushari is a dish of organised chaos. Rice, lentils, pasta, and chickpeas are each cooked separately and then combined. Two sauces go on top: a sharp, garlicky tomato sauce with vinegar and a darker oil with fried onion bits poured over everything. Every bite has multiple textures and temperature contrasts.

The dish sounds unlikely. In practice it is one of those combinations that work completely. The acidity of the tomato sauce cuts through the starchiness of the base. The crisp onion gives texture. The vinegar sharpens everything.
Small pasta shapes are traditional: elbow macaroni, ditalini, or broken spaghetti. The pasta is cooked and drained first, then mixed into the rice and lentil base.

items.prepNote: small shapes: macaroni, ditalini, or similar
poured into the onion oil just before serving

content.text: Cook the lentils, then the rice

Simmer the brown lentils in plenty of water for 20 to 25 minutes until just tender. Drain and set aside. In a medium saucepan, heat 1 tbsp oil, add the rice, and stir for 1 minute. Add 550 ml of water and a pinch of salt. Bring to the boil, cover, and cook over the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Remove from the heat and leave covered for 5 minutes. Fold in the cooked lentils and the chickpeas.
Boil the pasta in salted water until just cooked. Drain well and fold into the rice and lentil base.

Heat the olive oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the passata, vinegar, cumin, chilli flakes, and salt. Simmer for 10 minutes until thickened and sharp. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Fry the sliced onions in the vegetable oil over medium-high heat, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes until very dark and crisp. Remove with a slotted spoon. Remove the pan from the heat and add the vinegar to the hot onion oil; it will sizzle. Serve the rice base in deep bowls. Spoon tomato sauce generously over the top. Scatter the crispy onions and drizzle the vinegar oil over everything.

rows.symptom: Lentils mushy before rice is ready
rows.fix: Cook the lentils just until tender; they should still hold their shape. Drain them while still slightly underdone.

rows.symptom: Onions not crisp, just soft and dark
rows.cause: Heat too low or too much oil
rows.fix: Fry over medium-high heat. Spread the onions thinly in the pan so each piece gets contact with the hot surface.

rows.cause: Too much vinegar or acidic passata
rows.fix: Add a pinch of sugar and simmer for 2 more minutes to mellow the sharpness.

content.text: The classic kushari has no meat, but a version with spiced minced lamb added to the tomato sauce is served in some Egyptian households. The dish is endlessly adaptable; use whatever small pasta shape you have.

Each component stores well separately. The rice-lentil-pasta base can be refrigerated for 2 days; the tomato sauce for 3 days. Reheat and assemble fresh when needed. The crisp onions should be fried on the day.

Kushari shops in Cairo are a Cairo institution. They are found all over the city and have been feeding workers and students a cheap, filling lunch since the nineteenth century. The dish reflects the mixed history of Egyptian food: lentils and rice from an ancient tradition, pasta from Italian influence, the vinegar-and-tomato sauce from a later era. It is one of the most distinctively Egyptian dishes there is.
